content: Lymphatic filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by microscopic, thread-like worms. These adult worms reside exclusively in the human lymphatic system, which is responsible for maintaining the body's fluid balance and defending against infections. The disease is transmitted from person to person through mosquito bites. Individuals affected by lymphatic filariasis may develop lymphedema, elephantiasis, or, in men, swelling of the scrotum known as hydrocele. Globally, lymphatic filariasis is a leading cause of permanent disability. Those disfigured by the disease often face social stigma and rejection, and their inability to work due to disability negatively impacts their families and communities. Lymphatic filariasis has been affecting humans for thousands of years, with evidence suggesting its presence as far back as 1500–4000 years ago. The first documented description of its symptoms was recorded in the 16th century by Jan Huygen Linschoten during his exploration of Goa. The disease is transmitted when infected mosquitoes bite a human host, introducing infective larvae into the bloodstream. These larvae migrate to the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, where they mature into adult worms capable of producing microfilariae. The adult worms can live for several years in the lymphatic system. Female worms release microfilariae into the bloodstream, which can then infect biting mosquitoes. Within the mosquito, the microfilariae develop into infective third-stage larvae over 1 to 2 weeks. When the mosquito bites another human, the larvae are transmitted, continuing the cycle. Lymphatic filariasis is caused by nematodes (roundworms) that inhabit the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes of the human host. The primary causative agents are Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. Repeated mosquito bites over several months or years are necessary to acquire lymphatic filariasis. Individuals living in tropical or subtropical regions where the disease is endemic are at the highest risk of infection. Short-term tourists to these areas are at very low risk. Most individuals infected with lymphatic filariasis remain asymptomatic and never develop clinical symptoms, even though the parasite causes damage to the lymphatic system. A small percentage of infected individuals may develop lymphedema. Additionally, filarial infection can lead to pulmonary tropical eosinophilia syndrome. Clinical manifestations typically appear years after the initial infection. For diagnosis, serologic techniques offer an alternative to microscopic detection of microfilariae. Patients with active filarial infections often exhibit elevated levels of antifilarial IgG4 in their blood, which can be detected using routine assays. The development of an immunochromatographic card test (ICT) with high sensitivity and specificity for detecting Wuchereria bancrofti infection has simplified diagnosis. These test kits are commercially available and require only 100 μL of fingerprick blood, which can be collected at any time of day or night. Treatment for lymphatic filariasis involves the administration of diethylcarbamazine (DEC), a medication that kills the microfilariae circulating in the blood. While DEC does not eliminate all adult worms, it prevents infected individuals from transmitting the disease to others. However, DEC is not indicated for treating lymphedema or elephantiasis, as most individuals with these conditions are not actively infected with the filarial parasite. Physicians can obtain DEC from the CDC after laboratory confirmation of infection. Primary prevention of lymphatic filariasis involves avoiding mosquito bites through personal protective measures or community-level vector control. Periodic blood examinations for infection and initiation of recommended treatment can also help prevent the development of clinical symptoms.
